utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning, everybody. Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Prosecution today is represented today by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, Ms. Nikolic, and that's it. The witness is also here, present in the courtroom. Good morning to you, Mr. Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to conclude your testimony today. But before we do so, there is a couple of words to you, Madam Fauveau. We have seen, of course, your filings about the witnesses that have been withdrawn and the witness schedule for January. Do I take it that that will be it? In other words, after the second of those two witnesses in January, you will rest your case?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we will no doubt put a filing for the admission of certain documents through a written filing, but that will be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. And I reckon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. I reckon that that will more or less happen any time between the 21st and the 22nd of January, which means, Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Josse, that you should be prepared to start immediately after that. I mean, aim at those dates or at latest the following Monday, which will be the 26th, I think, or something like that. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Nothing to add at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you have a rough estimate now as to the estimated -- as to the length of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not really. Okay. Thank you. That's why you need the Christmas break to think about it, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We certainly do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. McCloskey. We wanted to communicate something to you. We will come to it later on. In the meantime, we are looking to finding the specific document number. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Now, we ended yesterday with -- where I had to interrupt you in your answer because we would have caused a scheduling problem with the next Court, so I think we should start over so you can hear that question again, and it was actually an awkwardly worded question. So let me just try to clear it up. It had two parts, and the first part was I'd asked you if, given it is the Prosecution's position, that on the afternoon and evening of 11 July the VRS was not -- didn't really know where the 28th Division was, how was it that you were able to pack up the coms van and go towards Bratunac. The next part of that question was, how did you do it without an order. But let's do the first part first and then we can -- I'll ask the question about the order again. So if you could just answer the first question.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, shortly before packing up the communications centre at the Pribicevac IKM whereby the Pribicevac point ceased to exist, the army of Republika Srpska in that sector of the front had general information that the main bulk of the 28th Division, and I am thinking about the armed soldiers, was grouping in the northwestern section of the enclave, from Srebrenica towards Konjevic Polje and Kasaba, and that they were intending to break through towards Tuzla with the main bulk of their forces. And a minor part of the forces because of disorganisation and difference of opinion, that part would go towards Zepa. We also had information that their own civilian population was ordered or given instructions to relocate to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. This is the information we had in the afternoon hours on the 11th of July. When -- in the afternoon, General Mladic left the Pribicevac IKM as well as General Mladic [as interpreted] and General Zivanovic, when they all went towards Srebrenica, listening to the development of the situation via the communications while I was by myself at the IKM, I concluded that the battle order of our forces had already advanced far forward and that now it was possible to create a situation that our units would be used in the fighting with the enemy column which probably intended to break out towards Tuzla. At that point, the existence of the IKM at Pribicevac - having in mind this development of the situation - became from a military and strategic point totally unjustified because the forward command post must jump forward in order to be able to successfully serve as a command post for future assignments. So being guided by this as well as by the fact that I would be in a position to be left in this vast area alone with my soldiers and perhaps in a way be faced with the problem of some possible groups that were trying to break through in that section, I probably reported to the command post communications centre in Vlasenica and told them that I was switching off my equipment and that I was going towards Bratunac. This was very logical for me. It was very logical for me, and when I arrived at Bratunac I understood that my commander of the IKM, General Krstic, was very satisfied with this move that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one short brief correction on page 4, line 5. Instead of the word "Mladic" it should state "General Krstic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Let's proceed. I take it you agree to that, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, I am sure he didn't say Mladic twice. If he did, it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, where did you get -- specifically where did you get the information that the -- or the location of the Muslim forces on the 11th of July? Where did you get that information from or who did you get that information from in particular?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was information received through intelligence action. Specifically, at the IKM at a distance of 150 metres from me there was a vehicle with a monitoring or tapping devices for enemy communications, and it was crewed, by the Drina Corps force surveillance platoon under the command of Captain Mirko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- he was for the needs of the Krivaja 95 operation, posted a listening post or a listening group which kept us informed any time they discovered an important message among the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, the interpreters didn't catch the name of Mirko. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mirko Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you received the information regarding the location of the Muslim troops from Mirko Petrovic or his team?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received the information from that crew of his that was at Pribicevac in a separate vehicle where they had their own equipment and antennas to listen in on enemy communications in the Srebrenica enclave. Other information we would receive personally from commanders who were in combat contact with the enemy where they were able with less precisions to see more or less in which section of the enclave the forces of the 28th Division were grouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, what did those commanders, those VRS commanders, which commanders told you on the 11th where the 28th Division was? For example, what did Vinko Pandurevic tell you where the 28th Division was on the afternoon or evening of the 11 July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders who happened to be in contact with the forces of the 28th Division, we were able to receive information about what they could actually see along the axis of their attack where the enemy was moving, to the left, to the right, or backwards. So the information that we would receive from the commanders were pretty sketchy, especially from positions of the Milici Brigade which was holding elevations at Ravni, Buljim, and Bracan. They didn't move from those positions to execute attacks. So they were able to notice better the grouping of those forces because that grouping actually was moving towards that sector of our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it's going to be really a long day if you can't focus on my question. My question was very simple. What did Vinko Pandurevic tell you about the location of the 28th Division on the afternoon or evening of 11 July, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He specifically didn't tell me anything what was where -- specifically, we just had general information that they were grouping in the northwestern section of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, my question was what, if anything, did Vinko Pandurevic report to you about the location of the 28th Division? I will insist that you answer my questions, please. I am not asking you about general information, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything specific because it was not his job to inform me about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did Krstic tell you, if anything, about the location of the 28th Division on the afternoon or evening of 11 July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't also have any obligation to inform me about it, so he didn't. I told you where I had the information from, and this information was something that was available more or less to all the commanders who took part in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, the chief of intelligence of the Drina Corps, tell about the location of the 28th Division on the afternoon or evening of 11 July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric knew what I knew because the information from the radio surveillance platoon first arrived to the IKM where I was, so we were informed at the same time of all the information; meaning, General Krstic, Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the second part of that question. I believe you testified on direct that you -- you did this without orders. Is that true? You just picked up this van and left without receiving any orders from anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why didn't you call General Krstic and ask him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps at that point in time going towards Srebrenica and probably after that towards Bratunac, General Krstic was not accessible from where I was for communication purposes, but for me this was quite a usual matter for me to be able to make a decision of that type myself, that was in the spirit of the overall purposes of the execution of the assignment itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember why you didn't call General Krstic and ask him? I don't want you to speculate. When start an answer with "perhaps" or "probably" or "maybe," that's not very helpful. So if you don't remember, fine, but do you remember why you didn't call Krstic to get his approval to move?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't call him about that because I believed that this was normal decision for me to make and that it was quite normal for me to start -- to follow him so that he could effectively command the units from the point in time when he, too, had left Pribicevac. I considered it quite normal, according to military logic, for the communications centre to move behind him or after him once he had left Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he had a Motorola with him, didn't he, Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic always, when he would go from the IKM, took a soldier of mine with him, a communications person, and that person with him had a communication device which was used for command within the units that were taking part in the Krivaja 95 operation. I do not recall anything about the Motorola because it was not a device through which I established any kind of communication with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sir, there is -- there is a photograph of General Krstic, I believe it's on the 11th of July, in Srebrenica and he's holding a Motorola. Does that help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That helps me to remember the fact that when I testified eight years ago, the Prosecutor showed me that photograph, and I said what I said just now, and that was that I did not organise any communications which would imply in their composition the use of Motorolas, because we soldiers did not consider them to be devices that could substantially assist us in the command of the operation because we had protected communications from commanders lower down and communications to the Drina Corps. I allow for the possibility that General Krstic, perhaps, took it from someone. He personally never had a Motorola that he carried with him. It's possible that he took the Motorola from someone purely in order to monitor some of the participants at a lower level such as the participants from his brigade. I think that was the 2nd Romanija Brigade where he used to be the commander, so he liked to be in touch with Captain Ljubo Eric, the commander of that combat group, for example, by listening to him on that line to congratulate him personally or to encourage him and so on and so forth. So that would be only in this aspect. He could not have had a Motorola in order to command the units that were subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He could have spoken to the 10th Sabotage Unit on the 11th of July over a Motorola, couldn't he, if they were within range?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes. Theoretically, he could have been able to if he had had the need to communicate with them because they did have Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the same would be true if he was within range of Ljubisa Borovcanin who -- and if Borovcanin had a Motorola he could have communicated with him too, if they had both gotten on the same channel, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, I said that General Krstic did not have a Motorola with him at all times as one of the devices to use to command the units. We all knew that those devices were very easy to listen to and to disrupt. He could have taken a Motorola from someone for a while to hear some lower level commanders and komandirs at some channels and to tell them his opinion. I theoretically allow for the possibility that at that point in time he could have had if he had the need and the authority to command the 10th Sabotage Detachment, but that detachment was not in the communications plan and was not in the plan for the Krivaja 95 operation. It appeared only on the 10th of July, and I don't know what sort of orders he could have had --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You are just rambling on. I asked you about Ljubisa Borovcanin. We don't need to get into the 10th, and we need to try to get specific and answer the question. It would be easier on you that way.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the special brigade, I don't know precisely where they were when they arrived in the Bratunac area, but I think they were in the Bratunac area which is quite a large range geographically; quite a large distance for those Motorolas. So I don't believe that General Krstic could have spoken to that unit in the Bratunac area using a Motorola because the technical conditions were not in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you some of the facts that have come out here and maybe it will refresh your recollection, and if it does, fine; if it doesn't, no problem. And I hope I will get these roughly correct. Ljubisa Borovcanin received an order from Tomislav Kovac to report to the General Krstic on the 11th of July with his units, and Mr. Borovcanin has told us that he did that and he went to the forward command post looking for General Krstic. And he said that he did that on the 11th of July when you were there and that Mladic was there. In addition, we have a receipt, I think it was shown to you in direct, from Mr. Borovcanin's driver, a guy named Jovicic, where he took receipt of the Drina Corps coms plan, and that receipt was found in the Drina Corps collection. So it's pretty clear from the facts in this case that Mr. Borovcanin was the same place that you were on the 11th, he was reporting to the VRS, and he received a coms plan. It's also very clear that he relied heavily on Motorolas because we see him with Motorolas on two days, the 12th and the 13th. So I don't know if that refreshes your recollection about Mr. Borovcanin, but perhaps -- does it? And if it doesn't, we'll go on.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely abide by what I said eight years ago, and this is correct, as regards what I know about the MUP unit which arrived in the Bratunac area on the 12th of July. I did not see them myself, or, rather, I didn't see them. I didn't see any of them at the forward command post. They were not in our communications plan, and we never established any communications from our communications plan with that unit while I was in that area. And that was the 11th of July at 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 412 up. And perhaps we can save a little time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You remember, I believe, Mr. Harmon in talking to you about this question of authority to move the command post asked you -- he pointed out to you the old JNA rules which required that for movement of command that there be authority given. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that what those rules say?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could take just a very brief look at page 38 in the English and page 60 in the B/C/S. And under this particular section, it says: "The command moves from one command post to another following the plan or in emergency, but always by decision of the commander and with approval of the senior officer." So was that rule in place when you, Major Jevdjevic, made the decision on your own to move the coms?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that rule was in place. It was functioning normally because we were a rather well-organised army. But whether in this rule or some other rule, initiative is permitted provided you have weighed the situation carefully and you are willing to take the consequences for a decision you make on your own initiative. Likewise, General Pandurevic released the prisoners at Ustipraca and opened up the corridor at Balkovica to have a column of the 28th Division allowed to pass through, and he was never held -- taken to task for that so that if you put a soldier in a trench, you don't have to tell him to shoot every time he sees an enemy approaching him. So this is simply gauging the situation, because if a situation in wartime appears, you have to adapt the rules to the combat situation and act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So are you saying that Colonel Pandurevic took prisoners at Ustipraca or is that a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may sound odd in the interpretation, but I wanted to draw a parallel between this decision, which I made on my own initiative, and the decision taken by General Pandurevic on his own initiative to let the Muslim column pass through Ustipraca without the approval of his superior command, this column consisting of civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we understand that Mr. Pandurevic apparently decided not to use his artillery and weaponry on the refugees leaving Ustipraca and we are happy that he made that decision, but you mentioned "prisoners of war." Was that just a slip of the tongue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, he didn't, he mentioned "prisoners "according to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't mention that. That is a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are you satisfied with that following the intervention of Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am, and I am also a bit concerned that some terms are getting a bit confused. This witness is being cross-examined on a document that relates to command centres and on the basis that he moved a communications centre. Is it the Prosecution's case that a command and a communications centre are the same thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to discuss this in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we all agree that the communications centre for a command is an essential part of the command and leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's your position. Basically what Mr. Haynes is interested in is knowing what your position is. So we can proceed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to go over with you the collection that the Prosecution has, it's a small collection of material that was sent -- we believe was sent from the Pribicevac forward command post and the material that we believe was received and just get a few of your thoughts, and try to keep your thoughts and answers as precise as possible, if you could. And could we start with 65 ter 4100. And I want to show you the original of this one. And if you could take a look at it and if we could put it on the ELMO. And I want you to specifically look at that signature. I think you have talked about this briefly in this case so it shouldn't be an issue, but -- and if you could hand that to the usher so they can put it on the ELMO, because as you can see, the scanned version of the original doesn't do the justice to the -- to the signature. Now, we can see from this document, I think you will agree, that it's from the Pribicevac forward command post, dated 5 July, and it's to the command of the Drina Corps' intelligence and security department, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's from Lieutenant-Colonel Svetozar Kosoric, the chief of intel of the Drina Corps, and it was sent to the Drina Corps intel department on 5 July at 1600 hours, according to the handwritten note, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature of your guy down here that signs this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This signature resembles all the other signatures of the cryptographer who was with me, and his name is Oliver Sekulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. And could you also look at that number, it looks like 0411-2, do you know what that is, what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about under "predato, Br.01.", do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my logistic, this could be the first telegram that Oliver Sekulic sent after our arrival at the forward command post. As I said, we arrived there on the 5th of July in the early afternoon and I conclude now that this might be the first telegram that he handed over or sent from that forward command post. This number, 04/1-2, is written in a quite different kind of pen compared to the one he used to sign his name, and I don't know who might have entered that number on the document and what it represents, but I'm certain it wasn't him. I don't know what that number means. Because -- well, maybe you can see that on the original -- I mean, you can see that on the original, maybe not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Let's go to the next one. It's 65 ter number 4111. We do not have an original of this. This was obtained from the Defence in the Krstic case. And again I just -- we see that it's from Pribicevac. It's sent on 6th July at 2115 hours, and that is again, if we are looking at the B/C/S version, that's Mr. Sekulic's signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to be able to see the originals, if possible, as I had this telegram, but I will try to assist to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's all I wanted to -- to confirm, and that -- well, that it was sent to both the Main Staff and to the Drina Corps command, correct? We can see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 4082.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again, we see this is, as it's up in the left-hand corner, from Pribicevac to the Drina Corps command, personally to the commander, which we will agree was General Zivanovic at the time, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Krstic sent this personal correspondence to General Zivanovic from which you can clearly see what I testified about last week, that these two brigades, the Milici and Bratunac Brigade, as I stated last week, it says "brigades that you commanded contributed the least to the success of the operation and by this you have offended those who are unstoppable on their way forward." So this only confirms that those units simply held the positions and engaged in a show of force. You are trying to convince me that that was not the case. In any case, this document was sent from the forward command post, and it was also signed by my cryptographer Oliver Sekulic, and this is the fist time I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's General Krstic just getting right in the face of his commander about something. Do you have any information that General Krstic was aware he was going to soon become the commander? How else could he talk like this to his commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dare comment on that because of my professional code of conduct. I am really not aware of this information. This was a new and surprising information for me. As I said yesterday, that in the heat of action, when the Drina Corps was engaged in major action, there was a change-over of commanders and that the Chief of Staff should be in charge of a hundred men, I spoke about this yesterday, but I see that you are not interested in hearing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I am listening to everything you are saying. I've just got the juggle the exhibits and several other things. So don't worry, I am listening to everything. I apologise, and standing up here for hours is not always most polite thing in the world. And I -- some of the information in these telegrams, you know, is important, though I may not be asking you a lot about it; though if you feel it's something important to your testimony, you can always talk about it. Let's go to the next one. We are now going to go to some of -- those are all our collection of sent documents. Now we have some that we believe were received at the Pribicevac forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter number 4101.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I -- I'll give you the original of that one so you'll have that advantage. Now -- and there is -- we see that it's from the command of the Drina Corps, the intelligence section, this is a bad translation. It says "information Section," it should be "Intelligence Section." And it's to quite a few people -- I mean units, but at the end we see Drina Corps IKM Pribicevac, inform the commander, and it's an intelligence report. And we are back now to July 5, so we are back to that first day you have mentioned, and it gives some informs about NATO and other things that I don't really want to ask you about right now. But it gives a background of Zepa, what's going on a bit -- what's going on there. But I want to focus you on the back. Is that -- again it says "Received 6 July at 1545 hours ..." And is that Sekulic again?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my cryptographer who was with me all the time and that is not in doubt at all. You told me that I might comment on something a little while ago, and I would like to very briefly in connection with this document. Last week, during my testimony, at one point I mentioned that my recollection as regards the organisation of communications in the Krivaja 95 operation, was that we had quite incredibly a lot of problems, a lot of interference and noise in the RRU-1 equipment. And you remember, I told you, if a telegram was rather long, like this one here, you see, because here on the screen you can see only one page but in the original, as you can see, it's a huge telegram. This telegram, in order to be sent through the communications centre, needed at least five minutes of high quality line, but there was often interference which would make the entire telegram collapse. And the encryptor would have to start all over again and repeat the sending of the telegram, and you can see up here where he wrote in his own hand, and you can see that clearly on the original, when a telegram is sent he put something called a pseudo-accidental sequence of impulses. These are signs which don't mean anything. And you can see three places I corrected in his own hand what these codes mean, and he had to do that when telephoning the communications centre of the centre -- of the sender. And he would say, what did it say in that sentence so that you don't have to repeat the whole telegram. And then he wrote two sentences in his own hand which had been destroyed by the interference on the line. And this is what I mentioned yesterday, that that was the first time we had a lot of noise in the channel and a lot of interference while communicating, and now I am pleased to have this before me where I can show you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's Sekulic's own hand that we can see on that original, handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because you see here there is a line of numbers and other signs. That's what the encryption device sends on the line, but that appears when there is noise on the line, and although this is not allowed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I understand, that's all I needed, just to confirm that that was Mr. Sekulic. And this document was received by Sekulic at Pribicevac at 1545 hours, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 4102. It's from the Drina Corps command to the Pribicevac IKM. And it's regarding the forwarding of an order, which I don't really want to ask you about. It's from General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you confirm that this was also received at the Pribicevac command post, and that's Sekulic's signature at -- so it was received at 2040 hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 4103. This is a document from the Drina Corps command intelligence department to many addressees, including the Drina Corps IKM, and it says "Pribicevac." And it's an intelligence report on that -- that first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you confirm that again this was received by Sekulic 6 July 1540 hours at the Pribicevac command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we scroll down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 207. And this is from the command of the Drina Corps, dated 7 July to the IKM of the Drina Corps, Pribicevac. This is the only addressee. And it's about the enemy activities in the enclave of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you confirm that that was received by Sekulic at the Pribicevac forward command post at 2240 hours, as we see in the bottom there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that Oliver Sekulic received that telegram on the 7th of July, and allow me to say here in the first sentence, it says here what you didn't believe me half an hour ago, "According to a report from our intelligence organ in the 1st Milici Brigade in the early morning hours, at about 0500 hours, from the observation post of the Bracan elevation, movements of enemy soldiers and civilians were observed." You remember when half an hour ago, I told you about the Bracan observation post in the area of the Milici Brigade and how the commanders of that brigade informed us of the movements of the enemy. You didn't believe me. This is first time I've seen the document, but every time I see a new document, it only goes to confirm what I previously said in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to argue about it, but it sounds to me like that this is observing from -- what's going on at the Zepa enclave, but this is dated the 7th of July so I don't think I -- we need to ask you anymore questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of July, it was the second day of combat actions in Srebrenica. That day nothing was done because of the rain and the fog, and probably you are now linking this with Zepa. But what I read about the Pracan observation post in the Milici Brigade area is probably consistent with what I talked about half an ago and you didn't believe me, and for the first time I am seeing this document and it confirms what I testified. This is what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, sorry to intervene, but from that comment I believe that there is a mistake in the English translation, because in the English text we can read: [In English] "Small group of civilians from the Zepa enclave." [Interpretation] And, indeed, what is written in the text in B/C/S is: "Small group of civilian population towards the Zepa enclave."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That would make more sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that there was civilians seen by the Milici Brigade going in the direction of Zepa on the 7th, is rather interesting. I've never heard it before. But let's not worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter number 4105.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Probably it's clear to everyone that the sentence says that the Milici Brigade was located towards Srebrenica. Pracan is also in the direction of Srebrenica. I know that area well, I spent years there. But all right, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think there is any question that on 11 July, 11, 12, 13 July that there were certain Muslims going towards Zepa. And the issues of when people knew about it and all is another issue, but let's -- let's get to that when we get to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's go to 65 ter number 4105, another document from the Drina Corps intel department dated 8 July, and it's to the forward command post at Pribicevac, the "Attention: Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric," and it's Vujadin Popovic. And it's talking about "the UNPROFOR position in Biljeg is still under our control."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't really want to ask you about that issue. I just want to confirm that this is again received on 8 July by Mr. Sekulic at 2115 hours, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 4106. This is from the Bratunac Brigade intelligence and security organ from Momir Nikolic, dated 9 July. And it's to three different parties, the Main Staff security administration, the Drina Corps security department, and the Pribicevac IKM Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. In this, they are talking about the DutchBat requesting a meeting with the representative of the Serbian side at Zuti Most. And can you just confirm that this again was received at the Pribicevac forward command post on 9 July at 1500 hours by Oliver Sekulic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter number 3018. This is from the Drina Corps command intelligence and security department, very urgent, to the Drina Corps IKM at Pribicevac, General Krstic personally, and to the Main Staff intel and security department, General Tolimir, personally, and it says it's from General Tolimir, interestingly enough. Now, can you confirm that this was received by Mr. Sekulic at 9 July at 2025 hours from his handwriting there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I won't ask you about the substance of that. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 6D00022. This is a document that is actually from the Drina Corps forward command post, Pribicevac, to the Main Staff and the Drina Corps command. And it's by General Krstic. You've talked about this document before, and sure you will agree with me that that is Mr. Sekulic's signature on this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there is - just for everyone's information, there is no ERN on this document. It was received from one of the Defence teams. And, sir, you have testified about this that this "received at 2320 hours" meant that it was received by somebody else at 2320 hours; is that correct? Not the Pribicevac forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am glad that it's the turn of a document of this nature. Other than the first one in the entire series of documents, all were documents that some of the part -- or one of the participants sent to the IKM, except for the first one from the 5th of July which talks about the document which was sent from the IKM to the intelligence organ of the Drina Corps. And it was coded or encrypted and Oliver Sekulic wrote "delivered." Now, this document of the 9th of July is also going from the Drina Corps IKM at Pribicevac and it's signed by General Krstic. But isn't it plainly obvious that the encryption person wrote in his handwriting "received." What does that mean? And he's handing the document over, but he wrote at the bottom "received on the 9th of July, 1995 at 2320 hours." I assume that you would put this set of questions to me, but I thought that we had clarified that eight years ago. I said that we had certain problems in communications and in the encryption because of disruptions when a telegram was sent out. He never knew, until the other side tried to decode it, whether they would manage to do that or not because of the interference. Then, they received an order so that he would be sure that the telegram was successfully dispatched, the other side would need to confirm that they received it and decoded it successfully and then the encryption personnel would receive that for the telegram that they sent out, they would need to make a note that it was received when the other communications centre reported back to them that it had been received successfully and decoded. I found this same telegram, the Defence showed it to me just by accident, that arrived at the command of the Drina Corps to which it was addressed, and specifically on that telegram the Defence has that telegram. They can give it to you. You can make a comparison. The encryption person wrote that he received this telegram at 2320 hours and he dictated that time to Oliver Sekulic when they spoke and then Oliver Sekulic was sure that his telegram was successfully dispatched in these difficult conditions, and then he wrote here "Received on the 9th of July, 1995, at 2320." The same telegram that arrived at the other side, the same time is written, 2320, and that is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I will agree with you that there is a received version of the document that was received at the Drina Corps that you are referring to. I will get the 65 ter number of that for the record. It's 6D -- no, I don't have that right now but I will get that. I agree with you, it does exist. But you will agree with me, I think, that this document was in fact sent from the Pribicevac forward command post on the evening of July 9th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, just as I am asking you to confirm whether in the received version the same time is written, affirming what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And it's the Prosecution's position that because we have seen many, many received documents, and we have never seen -- we've seen many received documents and we have never seen any mention like this noting the time it was received some place else, that if that was the case, instead of putting "received on 9 July 1995 at 2320 hours," they would have put "at the Drina Corps command," and they didn't. So it's the position of the Prosecution that this likely means that one of two things: Mr. Sekulic, like we all do, made a mistake. Instead of putting "sent" he put "received," or, because we don't have the original, somebody forged this for some reason. What do you think of those two options?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am still in that group of people who find it very hard if somebody does not believe what they are saying, and it effects me even more when I am testifying under oath before this Trial Chamber and somebody tells you that you have not been telling the truth for eight years. Perhaps my mental -- or my mindset cannot understand that, so I apologise to you. But all I am stating here are facts, because in 2008 when I discussed similar things about a telegram of the 12th of July, I remained by my assertion that the IKM and the communications centre left Pribicevac on the 11th, while Mr. Harmon showed me a telegram about -- where Oliver put his signature on the 12th. I still stood by what I said. I didn't understand the gist of that document, but I asked the Defence, they copied the document, I took it with me from The Hague and I couldn't wait to find the encryption person and to ask him what it was all about. And he explained the actual problems that the encryption personnel had and the instructions that they had, and this encryption person came on -- in 2001 and stated this explanation before the Court in the case of General Krstic, and I thought that in this aspect all the matters were crystal clear, but still I am here available to answer all of your questions nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdjevic, don't take it personally. The Prosecution's position is the same now as it was then, but you are jumping ahead of us a bit. The judges haven't seen that yet, and so they are probably not quite sure what we are talking about, but we are going to get to those documents, believe me. But let me say did you actually -- are you saying after you testified in Krstic, you went and talked to Mr. Sekulic about this document on 9 July or are you talking about the 12 July document that we will get to in a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go into private session just for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, the received version of this document that was received at the Drina Corps at 2320 hours is 65 ter 4083.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, just on this document, and we'll get to the 12th, on this document don't you leave open the -- the likelihood that Mr. Sekulic just made a mistake and wrote "received" when he should have wrote "sent," should have written "sent"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not allow for that possibility at all, because on all the documents, mostly from the 6th or the 7th when he was faced with this problem, there is a whole set of these documents that went out from the IKM. I think this one here is the 8th in order -- or in sequence, if you can see it -- well, I don't know who has the original. I think it's a 08/95, so it's the eight document. Probably it would be a good thing to analyse each one, since the time is consistent with the document time that it was received in the command of the Drina Corps. So obviously he was writing the word "primljeno," "received," here with the intention that it should mean that the act was successfully received at the end where it was supposed to be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one, it's 65 ter 4084. We jumped to the 11th, so we are getting closer. And I will show you the original if it will help, but this is -- like the others we have seen, it is from the Drina Corps. Now, this is the 4th RIV, the Radio Reconnaissance Platoon, dated 11 July, and it's distributed to the Drina Corps intelligence department and the forward command post, and it's from Lieutenant Petrovic who you've mentioned. And it is -- you'll agree with me this is Mr. Sekulic's signature again, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the signature of my encryption person, and it's a document received from the Drina Corps and it's evidently a document that arrived from another IKM to the IKM at Pribicevac. It's a receipt that, like I said today, that we received information from intelligence sources. And this is an information of such a nature coming from the Radio Surveillance Platoon from the corps command, and those who were close to us would provide this information to us by voice, not by act. And it indicates the intention of the forces of the 28th Division, and even in a sentence it says that the conversation was intercepted, and ultimately something is wrong, they intend to destroy the UN, and they are thinking of the units of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica. That's what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that, and you will agree with me that this was received by Mr. Sekulic at the Pribicevac forward command post on 11 July at 1530 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go to the next one, which is 65 ter 6D00207. We don't have an original of this. This was given to us by the Defence, Krstic. And -- however, we can see that this was from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps command and the Drina Corps IKM/1. It doesn't say "Pribicevac," unlike the others, but if we do look at it down at the bottom that's Mr. Sekulic's signature down there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that it doesn't say that it was addressed to the Pribicevac IKM, it says that it was addressed to the IKM/1 of the Drina Corps, in view of the fact that at that time the Drina Corps had only one IKM and that was the one at Pribicevac. It means that -- I have no doubt that this is the Pribicevac IKM and also because the signature of my encryption person is here, that he received the document at 1735 hours. I remember this document very well, as compared to some other ones, because at the time I read it myself and I read it because at that time there -- General Mladic, General Zivanovic, or General Krstic, or Colonel Vukota were not at the IKM. So as the communications person, I was the only officer present at the IKM at the time, so my encryption man at the time, because he had a certain deadline in which he had to dispatch priority telegrams, and it does say "very urgent" here, it is his assignment to dispatch -- or to deliver the telegram immediately to the person it was addressed to. Since no one was there who had command responsibility to receive the telegram and to read its contents, he asked me what he should do, because he was not permitted to hold a telegram without delivering it, without passing the telegram on, because it was a very urgent one. So I read this telegram purely to see which issues it was dealing with, how urgent it was, in order to be able to intervene. And I was very glad to read a very civilized and military inclined view of General Gvero about the treatment by our forces of the UNPROFOR where there is a sentence that the UNPROFOR and the civilian population should be treated in the spirit of the convention. And then it says "Regardless of their behaviour, regardless of their extreme behaviour, unfavourably extreme behaviour by UNPROFOR, that they should be treated in a civilized and proper manner," as should be the case for the civilian population as well. So I remember this document very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you agree then that General Gvero is instructing through the subordinate commands that the Drina Corps ensure the utmost correct treatment of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he issues these instructions. Ultimately, it is part of his duties and matters that were in his jurisdiction, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you think General Gvero had the authority to issue instructions to the entire corps like this, to the corps people referred to in this -- in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for whether he had that authority or not, I don't know, but I know that it was within his purview to deal with UNPROFOR and the relations with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So whether -- whether he had it or not, he was using his authority, wasn't he, when he did -- sent this instruction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are a little concerned about the terminology used here. My learned friend used the word "introduction," the document says "warning." We say there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you mean I used the term "instruction."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I called it what I thought it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. I think it's clear that we can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, so, whether he had the authority or not, let's not quibble. Let's -- you will agree with me he was using the authority of his position to send this document and this instruction to the units in it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that part and I wouldn't wish to speculate, but I did agree with this opinion more or less, so I just remember that particular telegram. As for who had instructions and authority within the Main Staff is something I don't know. I just know that it was within his purview to deal with cooperation with UNPROFOR and contacts with journalists and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you -- did you feel as a major in the VRS that you were obligated to follow his instruction in this and treat UNPROFOR fairly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we, according to my information, did that. Even without this instruction, the instruction was just there in order to affirm some of my thinking and commitment in that sense, and that's why I was glad that this was being materialised on paper. This is why I remembered this document. The document reflected my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- and we are all happy about this, but did you feel obligated to follow this document? Did you feel obligated to follow the instruction of General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the document did not affect me. I had my commander whose orders I implemented, so the document in some kind of sense of an order did not include me. It just touched me in the sense that I also shared the same lines of thinking as reflected in this document. In the army there is a hierarchy, so I had my own commander superior to me so that his orders would affect me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's the time. We can have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one minor matter. Mr. McCloskey, page 29, line 24, you indicated that the received -- the 65 ter number of the received version of the controversial document was 65 ter 4083. I couldn't locate it. Could you check it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And before we rise, Judge Prost would like to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted to alert the parties, specifically the Prosecution and the Borovcanin Defence team, that at the conclusion of the evidence from this witness later this morning, we would like to hear the comments of both the Prosecution and the Borovcanin Defence team specifically and solely on the issue related to the pending motion that focuses on two documents, excerpts of P210 and P3838. And the only point we would like to hear oral submissions on with respect to that motion is in relation to the excerpts of P210 in relation to Rules 89(c) and (d); that is specifically the arguments of both parties on relevance, probative value, and any possible prejudicial effect to fair trial flowing from those -- that one particular document. So we would be expecting oral submissions on that single point later this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. McCloskey, how much longer, if I may ask, just to know where we stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope I can finish in a couple of hours. We are at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- the place we were trying to get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We just wanted to know where we stand, that's all. We are not cutting you short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Judge Kwon, it's now there. It hasn't been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I got the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go now to 65 ter 438, and it's a two-pager, Colonel, so you may find this easier as well. This is a document Mr. Harmon showed you, and this is not -- we don't have any version that was received at Pribicevac. This has a big stamp on it. As we see on the back page, it has received at 2230 hours, processed at 2250. But it was sent, as I think you will agree with me, from the Drina Corps command on 11 July, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was sent from the command of the Drina Corps on the 11th of July at -- and it was processed at 2250 and immediately after that, forwarded to all the units as mentioned here. As the corps commander, Major General Zivanovic was not at 2200 hours on the 11th of July, he was not at the corps command at that time. Colonel Pedrag Josic signed for him. I recognise this signature. And this document was not received at the Pribicevac forward command post for the simple reason that there was no communications centre at the time at Pribicevac, so the document could not have been received there. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see what it's about. It actually has to do with -- it's entitled "Order to block the linking up of the forces of the 28th enemy division with the forces in the enclaves." I don't think I will ask you if this information is -- is consistent with what you've been saying or not, unless you would like to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there is any need to read the document now. I don't know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it's about the 28th Division, and it's an order to block them. And I believe it looks like they are worried about the 28th Division returning from a battlefront to the Srebrenica area, to come into the backs of the VRS forces. There is no talk in here of the 28th Division taking off towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're wrong, Mr. Prosecutor. I'm sorry I didn't read the document at once. One should read every document right away, but it says quite precisely here: "The command of the 28th Muslim Brigade from Srebrenica asked to go back from the Sarajevo war front." So this is about Naser Oric, and perhaps a few of his officers, and it's quite incredible that you are saying that the 28th Division was at the Sarajevo war front when it says quite clearly that only the command was there. And this refers primarily to Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's Naser Oric in the command, he's what I meant to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next document. It's 65 ter number 439. It's the -- I'm sure you will agree with me, it's same document as the other one, basically, 11 July, confidential number 03/1574, which is the same one we just saw. However, this one, we can see a very familiar Mr. Sekulic. So this was --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you show me that page, please? Or, if you have a document in hard copy it would be even more useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, they can blow that up for you on the screen to make it a little bit bigger so you can see the signature, but I am sure you will agree with me that this is the same document and this is the receipt version of the document, where Mr. Sekulic says -- and this is -- well, let's see who it is addressed to. It is addressed to the IKM forward command post. It does not specifically set out Pribicevac. But we recognise -- I am sure we recognise the signature of Mr. Sekulic. And it says, "Received 11 July at 2350 hours."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, as it doesn't say "Pribicevac forward command post," I agree with you that it refers to that document. And it says down here that the document was received by him at 2350. That's that time. You probably want me to comment on how this was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the time I mentioned in my testimony seven and eight years ago and in the course of last week, when, together with the cryptographer, and the communications centre, I arrived in the command of the Drina Corps at Vlasenica. From the point in time when we left the Pribicevac forward command post at about 1900 hours on the 11th, my cryptographer no longer had the technical conditions he needed to receive or send documents. In the meantime, documents arrived for the communications centre somewhere, but he was unable to receive them. So those documents piled up in other communications centres because they were unable to forward them to us. This document is such a document. On behalf of General Zivanovic, who was attending a meeting at Bratunac at the time, it was signed by Colonel Pedrag Josic, but the communications centre of the Drina Corps was not able to hand this over to Sekulic because Sekulic was already travelling with me from Pribicevac towards Bratunac and then on to Vlasenica. When we arrived at the forward command post of the corps at Vlasenica, of course I reported to the operations centre and he to the communications centre. And then he was able to receive this document at 2350 when it was handed to him from the communications centre of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, because that communication centre had to hand over this document to all the addressees listed here. And he took the opportunity only when we returned to Vlasenica to hand this document over to the cryptographer for him to distribute. He was unable to send it to him through a technical communications equipment. He handed it over to him physically, and then he stated here that he received this document in Vlasenica at the time mentioned here, at 2350, and this corresponds fully. And that's my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So this was printed out at Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so the print -- the teleprinter that printed this one is different from the teleprinter that was at the Pribicevac forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At Pribicevac we had two kinds of teleprinters. One was working and the other one was a reserve, but they were of two different makes and one can recognise this by the shape of the letters. This is an electronic teleprinter produced -- well, it was called ETL1. It was the Nis Electronic industry that produced it. The other teleprinter which we happened to have in reserve was produced by Siemens, it was of the mechanical time, and the letters are quite different. They're like small written letters and it's T100. That's the type of teleprinter it is. So you will see that on the 5th and 6th of July, the documents sent by Svetozar Kosoric from Pribicevac, Sekulic, the cryptographer used the mechanical teleprinter. And when one was working, the other one was used as a reserve. Or when he was typing on one he was using the other one to decrypt the message. That's how he worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified that documents came to the Drina Corps command were piling up there and that when you guys got to the command, those documents were given to Sekulic and he -- well, this particular one, he signed and received, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pedrag Josic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... so this document was printed out by a machine at the -- in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Sekulic arrived the machine printed this out, and he was handed this document personally, because before that there was no technical means for the document to be sent to him and it was intended for him as cryptographer at the Pribicevac forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you said these documents had been piling up waiting for him and when he got there, they were handed to him. Now you're saying it was printed out after he was there. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understand, the cryptographer -- if you knew the technique you wouldn't be putting this question. When the cryptographer prepares this document for all the units, it's a long strip of paper, a long narrow strip of paper, and he sends this to all units, all units, and he encircles the unit to which it has been sent. And probably only the Pribicevac forward command post was left over. It had not been sent to them. And when Sekulic turned up in the evening of the 11th at that communications centre, this is military discipline. He reports and he says, I was absent, do you have any telegrams for me. Or, perhaps, the encryptor of that communications centre rang him up and said, Hey, where have you been, I have several telegrams for you. And then he took that tape, or, rather, that long narrow strip of paperer, he put it through the machine, the machine typed this out, he signed it, and then he handed it over. Because the cryptographer at the Vlasenica centre had to sign in his report that he had sent the document to all the units. That's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this document that was at Vlasenica, was it printed out before or after Sekulic got there, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those are details which are so irrelevant as far as I am concerned. It's just as irrelevant as the question whether I entered this courtroom by that door or this door. I am answering your questions, of course, but there was a possibility if that cryptographer knew - and he must have known - that we were leaving Pribicevac, he might have typed this out beforehand to hand it over to Oliver Sekulic. Or when Oliver Sekulic arrived he might have printed it out then and handed it to him. Those are just logical conclusions I am drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But it was printed out on a Drina Corps teleprinter, not the forward -- former forward command post teleprinters, right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's logical, yes, in the communications centre of the Drina Corps. The teleprinters were the same. We used the same teleprinters. We had the same ones both in the Drina Corps and at the forward command post. It's a machine. The machines are the same, just as rifles are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a -- probably a good comparison, because you know you can determine whether a -- if you get a good bullet sample whether a bullet is fired from the same or a different rifle, and I think it's the same thing for teleprinters. And we'll go check and get back to you on whether or not this document is the same teleprinter as is at the Pribicevac forward command post or one from someplace else. We'll let you know. I don't know the answer to that right now.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll assist you to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This -- I think I have got an original for you which, if you want it. We'll see that this is from the Drina Corps command, the 4th RIV, we have heard about them before. It's dated 12 July. And we have that little handwritten business again, 04/1/50 written in some ink up on the right-hand side. And this is to -- specifically to the Drina Corps intelligence department at the Pribicevac forward command post. And it's an interim report. And they're listening on a particular frequency, and they know that these -- their intercept guys have concluded that this is Naser Oric's men, we can see. This is also -- isn't that Sekulic's signature there on the original one?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he received that 12 July at 0740 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And interestingly enough, your intercept guys say that "By monitoring this network, we reached the conclusion that they were all present, that they were heading in a direction unknown to us as yet, together with the people and their groups." So your monitoring guys don't know what direction they are going in at that point, I take it, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This intelligence information and the date is the 12th of July, and it's in the early morning, 4.30, our intercept - as I don't know what group it was - sent information to their commander, Mirko Petrovic in Vlasenica, and this information in my view fully reflects the situation of the 28th Division in the night between the 11th and the 12th. It says that the participants are known as Naser's men, komandirs, and the signalsmen, and group intercepting them concluded that they were moving towards us along an unknown axis together with people, civilians and their groups. So this is the information received from the surveillance group. The units he was listening in to didn't say they were heading in a direction unknown, but the people listening in were unable to determine by listening to the conversation at 4.30 what direction they were heading in. So it's only one of the conversations they listened in to and they were unable to pinpoint the direction in which these people were heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is this reconnaissance unit, is this coming from the Drina Corps command or from the truck down the -- or the truck that was at Pribicevac? Do you know where this is come from? It says Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely because the 4th Reconnaissance Platoon had several points at various trig points where they listened in. I know only about the one at Pribicevac, where they were during the operation, but where the other points were, I don't know. And where this group was that sent this report, I don't know. They may have been at Pribicevac or somewhere else, at Bracani for example. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's fair to conclude that Mirko Petrovic thought that the Drina Corps intelligence department was present -- was still present at Pribicevac, right? That's why he addressed it to him there, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He sent this on the 12th. I allow for the possibility that he thought that the forward command post and the communications centre still existed at Pribicevac. That's quite logical, because in the evening at around 2400 hours we arrived at Vlasenica, he was probably asleep, and at 4.30 in the morning his men discovered this and sent this telegram. And as you can see my cryptographer signed that he received this document at 7.40. Some time has to elapse for the telegram to be written, typed out, encrypted, sent, so all that took place before 7.40. And in the morning I am absolutely sure that when we woke up in the morning of the 12th, in the meantime, another telegram arrived for Sekulic. But he was no longer at Pribicevac, he was now in Vlasenica. He had arrived there, and then the cryptographer simply typed out, he used the ETL teleprinter, he put that long narrow strip of paper through the machine, and he thus fulfilled his obligation as regards this telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this type-face should not match the teletypes received in Pribicevac? It should come from a Drina Corps teletype where you say it was received?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This very important reconnaissance unit, a key part of the intelligence operation, doesn't know where the Drina Corps intelligence department is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Objectively at that point in time, Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric was the chief of intelligence. I assume that he spent the night between the 11th and the 12th at Bratunac. This was only one night. At that point in time they did not know that we were not at Pribicevac, but as soon as we turned up in the morning and had a rest, on the 12th, as soon as we woke up they knew we were here and they handed him this information straight away. That is logical. And the contents of this information fully reflect what was happening as regards the 28th Division in the night between the 11th and the 12th. Had the content been different, you might have had more arguments to impute to me. But this fully corresponds to what was actually happening in the night between the 11th and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kosoric was seen on video in Potocari on the 12th of July. So does that help refresh your recollection where he was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't deny that, but it says here "deliver to the intelligence department of the command of the Drina Corps," and underneath it says "Forward to the Pribicevac forward command post." Whether Kosoric as the first one listed here received this or not, I am not interested in that. What matters is that Sekulic where it says "Pribicevac forward command post" received it. He may have been -- Kosoric may have been in Potocari on the 12th, I don't know. I am only telling you what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to the next one, 65 ter 4086. It might have the original. This is from that same group, the reconnaissance folks, they are sending this to the Drina Corps command intelligence department, the IKM Pribicevac. And it's difficult to tell, maybe you can help us, whether they are addressing this to the Drina Corps command intelligence department at the IKM in Pribicevac or it's got two addressees; one the Drina Corps intelligence department, and two, the IKM Pribicevac. Can you tell from looking at this which one it is? The last one, I think it was a little clearer in the original.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth the Drina Corps has one intelligence department, or squad. Whether the person who sent this wanted to put the title and the location or whether he thought it was understood that Svetozar Kosoric was at Pribicevac at the time, I don't know. He may have assumed or known that Svetozar Kosoric was at Pribicevac and he might have thought he was at that forward command post. I don't know. I can't think of -- well, I don't know what I might have assumed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just -- there is a couple of mistakes in the English on this. It's -- I think you will agree that this is Mirko Petrovic, not Potrovic. And the received on 12 July 1995 should be "0745 hours"; is that correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I think that the previous one was at 0740, this one was at 0745.
