So probably just as long as it needs for the telegram to go through the machine and then he would sign one and then the other one. But, yes, that is time that's written there and you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, it is the position of the Prosecution that Mr. Sekulic is still at Pribicevac receiving this material as addressed to him at Pribicevac at the time in question. But I think we understand your explanation, it remains the same, we just differ on that, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can respond to some other things with "I think" or "I believe" or something like that, but specifically yesterday when we talked snipers, had you asked me, for example, if I ruled out any possibility that some sniper hits were directed at the enclave during the four years of the war, I would say -- well, my information is that I didn't see it. We usually didn't have such weapons. But perhaps some shot was fired. I cannot say otherwise. But as for the IKM communications centre at Pribicevac and the dismantling of the IKM on the 11th and the meeting at the Bratunac command on the 11th in the evening, do I not allow for any possibility that it did happen in some other way. That's as much as I would like to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, but like the sniper story, there are some more documents to look at and maybe I will bring you around on that. So keep your mind open and let's keep going through the documents. Here is another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter number 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And maybe the original will help you, I think we have it. Interestingly, on this one we see Sekulic's familiar signature. I think you will agree with me on that, won't you? I can show you the original so it's a little clearer. Is that -- that's Mr. Sekulic receiving this on 12 July at 1620 hours?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. Can you just allow me a little bit of time to read the contents of the telegram because that always helps me a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please. And just as background, we saw that just there was a one-liner in the previous one reporting that someone -- that the people -- I'm sorry. People entered a minefield somewhere is the previous one, to give us factual background to this one.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, previously, as I said, it does absolutely accord with the development of the situation in the field. I am prepared to comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you've already agreed with me this was received by Oliver Sekulic, and you will agree with me that it was sent by the command of the Drina Corps intelligence department on 12 July, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, the intelligence section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good. And it's very urgent, for immediate delivery, meaning it shouldn't be old news. This should be new news, right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are fresh news that they received or news that were Collated by the intelligence department from the listening groups. I see that Pavle Golic is the one who signed this document. So he put together all the information that arrived in the meantime and he is sending it out to all of those he thought would require that information, that they would need to know this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But now on the topic we've been on, we see -- we don't see anymore discussion of the Pribicevac forward command post. We see a Drina Corps Bratunac forward command post. And so now we have a Mr. Sekulic receiving a telegram that is addressed to the Bratunac forward command post, and it's our position that now Mr. Sekulic has moved. He is now at Bratunac, and he is receiving this information as we see it before us, that the Drina Corps intelligence department knows precisely where Sekulic and his coms people are and they are sending it to him there. Do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far you are asserting that the IKM at Pribicevac remained until the 12th, and now you're assuming that on the 12th it was in Bratunac. But, actually, this is what is involved. Intelligence man Pavle Golic does not need to know where Sekulic is. He would need to know where his superior is, Krstic. So he is sending this to Krstic. On the 12th, he knew very well that we were no longer at Pribicevac, but he also knew that General Krstic was in Bratunac, which is also correct. I am not disputing that. It is the result of all of my testimony. And he is sending the telegram to Bratunac in the belief that the telegram would be given to Krstic. On the 12th, as I testified, I myself and my communications people were already at the Krivace IKM in Zepa. So I said there on the afternoon hours of the 12th I had already arrived at Zepa, and this telegram was received by Oliver Sekulic in Zepa at 1620 hours. So this is the only possibility that I would allow, that he received this telegram at Zepa on the 12th of July at 1620 hours because that's when we were in Zepa already and the communications centre had been already set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, and you -- we see that 04/1-52 written up in the right-hand corner of the original, and you don't know what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it means, but I assume that it just could have been, if that's of any help, that some time later after the operation all the telegrams are redistributed. And then when Oliver came back after the Zepa operation and he was placing all the telegrams in their proper places and those who were given the telegrams later, perhaps Kosoric, when they were handing over the telegrams, then because of the records the telegrams should be logged in for a record. I guess this is what this is about, but all I am talking about is the actual receipt of the telegrams because this is something that I am well familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you must recall that General Krstic, in his testimony, said that there was this big meeting on the 11th of July that you've mentioned and that the orders were received to go to Zepa the next day. And surely you remember that General Krstic testified he did go to Zepa on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity to follow the General's testimony, and I don't know what he said, but I know what I said and I know how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just be clear. Are the Prosecution asserting that what General Krstic said is the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I am not. He was not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then what's the purpose of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the position of the Prosecution that this witness is very familiar with General Krstic's accounts and that, as a Defence witness for Krstic, aligned his testimony with General Krstic's account. And it appears that when Vinko Pandurevic interviewed Eileen Gilleece, his account was aligned on these issues. And so that's why all of this, I am spending so much time with it, just so it's clear what the Prosecution's position is and where we are coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You can safely proceed along this line, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think the question's been asked and answered and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. What I mean to say is that if you have further questions on this business in this area, you may safely put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I hadn't intended to go back in time anymore, but I think that that should do it. I can always provide the Court we with any background or any -- the testimony related to General Krstic if that would be helpful. All right. It may become more relevant down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's -- let me catch my breath and see where we are. All right. Now, let's go to another document, 65 ter 148. And let me give you the typed version of that. This is a long one from General Tolimir, and I am not so interested in the content. And I think you will agree with me that it's from the Drina Corps intelligence section to the Main Staff intelligence and security and to the intelligence administration, the Drina Corps IKM, General Krstic personally, the Drina Corps IKM Bratunac, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic [sic], personally. Now, this one, we don't have Mr. Sekulic on. We don't -- I think we don't have him. And I just for completeness wanted to show the Court and yourself these other telegrams that went to various IKMs. The one that says "Drina Corps IKM Pribicevac," actually, it says "Pribicevac." So we can conclude that -- or can we conclude -- what, if anything, can we conclude about that? This is addressed to Krstic at Pribicevac on the 12th, and we see that stamps on this thing, and the 2210 hours. It's a little hard to say if it's received or processed but ...

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first page, is it completely authentic as regards this telegram? I would like to have an original -- I mean, the original, because it's copied. I am trying to find my way here. Do you happen to have the original perhaps, or, if you say that this is an authentic copy, then I have no reason to not believe you. I would just like an answer so that I could make my comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have an original. We don't have originals of everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's just line 14 of the transcript, Mr. McCloskey asserted this document is addressed to Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic personally. I wonder if he could look at it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, if I've said that, that's a complete mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had the time to at least read some of the contents to see if that corresponds to that day, but it probably does. What this is about is this: This, to the first command, is the heading of the Drina Corps command intelligence section, strictly confidential, so on and so forth, and it's dated the 12th. So the intelligence section of the Drina Corps very urgently is forwarding a telegram that it -- that was earlier received from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska from the sector for intelligent questions. So it is just forwarding an earlier received telegram in its entirety and it's just adding the heading, its own heading, that of the Drina Corps command. I think everyone can see that very well. Unfortunately, the time is not stated here. When the telegram was drafted at the main staff, there is no date either. But I assume that this was also something that took place on the 12th of July. Probably, the person who drafted this telegram at the intelligence affairs sector at the Main Staff thought that at the time the IKM of the Drina Corps was still at Pribicevac. I am assuming that is why he put it here, but the is not something that the Drina Corps command wrote. Earlier on we discussed a document where the same intelligence section of the Drina Corps forwarded a telegram to Bratunac, so they already know that Krstic is in Bratunac. So why would they on the 12th, in the evening - you can see that it's 2210 hours - again return that telegram to Pribicevac if in the morning some of the telegrams had been sent to Bratunac. So my answer, in the end, is that this is just a telegram that was passed on from the Main Staff where somebody on the 12th at the intelligence sector in the main command still believed that the IKM was at Pribicevac and that's why they put it there, on the document. This is what I am -- would like to say about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I, to the extent that you have said that this is an indication that this sender, General Tolimir, doesn't really know where the coms centre is at this point, I agree with you, that the Prosecution's position that the coms centre in is in Bratunac and it's on its way to Krivace. And this an example of what you have said before is that the sender doesn't always know where the person is that he is sending something to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let's go to 65 ter 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let me give you that one. That's another -- it's not a -- we don't have Mr. Sekulic on this one, so this is similar to the last one. It's another Tolimir document sent to Pribicevac, General Krstic, and Bratunac, Colonel Popovic, just a little bit -- it looks like it's a little bit later than the last one. So I don't think I need to ask you anymore questions on that, it's so similar to the last one, unless you would like to make a comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is the same as of the previous telegram. It's a document that came from the Main Staff to the command of the Drina Corps. At the Drina Corps command they wanted to have this information or data to the units, so the heading is placed at the top and it's forwarded to the units as soon as possible, and I am very glad that you noticed that the person sending out the documents would not necessarily need to know where the person to whom the document is addressed is exactly located. So what's important is that the communications centre is addressed and then whoever is there at the communications centre will find the person, and this is a key piece of information, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to -- let's go to Zepa, let's go to Krivace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you have talked about this, I don't think you've -- I think you told us that you didn't see the -- this is the Zepa attack plan that General Krstic still did as Chief of Staff on the -- dated the 13th of July. You might want to just take a look at it. I just want to call our attention to it, because we now have a document that is from the Drina Corps command, the Krivace forward command post. I can't really tell from the material where this came from. I should know that, but I don't. But, do you recall sending out an attack plan to the various units involved in it from the forward command post on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you recall whether it was done, not whether you personally did it, but it should have been done according to this document, right? Do you recall it happening? You were there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th in the evening, the Krivace IKM was visited by Colonel Vicic. He was an operative who took part in the Krivaja 95 operation, together with General Krstic. On the 13th in the evening he --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... explain your answer, but if you give us the answer first, then we will know where you're going with your explanation. So the question is, do you remember sending this document out or somebody from the coms unit sending it out?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document, I don't recall if it was sent from the communications centre, but I remember that on the 13th in the evening, Colonel Vicic came to the Krivace IKM and he had these documents for the units that were taking part in the operation of Operation Stupcanica 95, whether any of these documents - and perhaps this order - could have been one of them went out to the units via the communications centre, is something I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell from the type whether that -- that copy I gave you is a teletype that would be sent or received, or could that be something that was, you know, couriered around, like by Vicic or someone?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was typed out. These are not teletype letters in either of the documents. I assume that the units in the Stupcanica 95 operation received these documents by courier or Colonel Vicic went to hand them over, the documents at the time when they were arriving from the Srebrenica sector to the Zepa sector to their staging sectors. I think it very unlikely that such a long document would be sent out by teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It's also possible you hadn't had the teleprinter working or it hadn't been up yet, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having any time intervals when the teleprinter was not working. We did have interference in transmission, but it continuously operated as means of communication, the teletype.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I want to go to 65 ter 2670B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I just want to focus for a second. There is an -- well, I think we should get the original for this. If we don't -- I'm sorry, we don't have that. But we can see from this that it is from the -- the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade to the various people, including the IKM Drina Corps, Krstic personally. And it's about Zepa and UNPROFOR locations. And can we go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, could we have a translation reference, please I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I will get there, but I don't want to confuse the issue because we have another version of this that is in English and we'll -- we'll get there, but I want him to look at the end of this first, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we should just be given that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In a minute, if you could just wait ten seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- I understand he may have his good reasons, so ten seconds is not going to make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you -- just let me give you the photocopy of this, and if we could show the bottom of the -- of this. Is this Mr. Sekulic again?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's his signature. I wish I had the original of the document here, but undoubtedly this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we have at 65 ter 2670, I believe it's the sent version of this document. So it's in English and it should be identical. What we are looking at now is the received version of it. I'm sorry I don't have the received version in English, but you will confirm for us that this was received by Mr. Sekulic at the Krivace forward command post, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this document corresponds to the original on the 14th of July, we were at Krivace, the document is addressed to General Krstic at the IKM. And I have no reason to doubt that he received this at Krivace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see in the handwriting corner, 04/ and now we see a 2. Before, we had been seeing 04/1. Do you know if there is a significance? Is it possible one is Pribicevac and 2 is Krivace?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I don't know what -- whatever is written up here means, but I don't think 1 refers to Krivace and 2 to another location, but really I don't know what these numbers up here mean. I assume they are markings from a logbook when documents are issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 4112, that's B. And there is an English at 4112, but we have the same issue. The English is the -- I believe the English is the received version, and I believe the B/C/S 4112B is the sent version because we see this word, I think it's "predato."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that sent?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't see what it says down here. I don't think anyone in this courtroom can decipher this writing. After the first two letters, it looks as of if it's been internationally scribbled over or scratched out. I really can't see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you will agree that the first two letters are "PR" and the last letter is "O"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only see on the screen when it blown up that the first two letters are "PR." I absolutely agree, but what rest of the word is, is it correct when you say "predato," "handed over," or "primljeno", "received," that, I can't see. Because it's first time that I can see that something is internationally corrected on a document. That's why I always like to see the original. Even someone who speaks Serbian perfectly cannot decipher this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Focus on the handwritten part and try to zoom in, please, as much as you can. We can try again once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I dare assume it says "primljeno," "received," because we can see a do the on the "i" and the last two letters could be "NO" which would mean that this is the usual way cryptographers wrote that they had received something. So it's probably "primljeno" and not "predato." But really, no one here in this courtroom can decipher that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, but we can see that it is from the command of the Drina Corps IKM Krivace, and we can see that it is to the GS VRS. So if it's being sent by Krivace to the VRS, this should be a sent, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a similar version of the writing of the cryptographer Sekulic is something we discussed earlier today, and I explained this to you and you confirmed this with documents, and when he received a confirmation from the communications centre to whom he sent the telegram that they had successfully received it, then he would write "primljeno." What we have here is a specific situation, rather unusual, because the document was sent to the Main Staff and the command of the Drina Corps. And he -- well, the Main Staff was not commanding these operations, so he had to send it through the Drina Corps to the Main Staff indirectly, because to avoid a lower level units, bypassing their immediate superiors and trying to contact their second superiors, they did not have the codes. They could not send things to the Main Staff except through the Drina Corps, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 4095. This is a document that appears to be original from the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to be able to give you the original, sir. And I am sure you will agree with me that this is the calendar for work days for your unit. And we can see that you're the first person on the list, a Major Milenko Jevdjevic, and we can see that in the remarks section you went to Pribicevac and Zepa. And then if we go down the list we see that Momir Bakmaz also went to Pribicevac and Zepa. We also see that Oliver Sekulic went to Pribicevac and Zepa. Then we go to the next page, and we see Veljko Vukosavljevic went to Pribicevac and Zepa, as did Mirko Plakalovic and Slavisa Ilic and Milorad Stevic. So that's you and six people, which is about what you said, and I am told that the names that you gave us the other day, you got about four of them right, which is pretty good, considering. And my question is, sir, you can see better than anyone that somebody has handwritten in, I can't tell if it's pencil or pen from my copy, but a hard bar between the 12th and the 13th for all those people. And -- I'm sorry, I misread the last two, Slavisa Ilic and Milorad Stevic went to Pribicevac and Trnovo, and -- sorry, and then Stevic went to Pribicevac and Kocar. And their Xs, those last two guys, stop at 12 July. And it looks like they get a couple of days off and they are off to Trnovo and Kocar. So it just appears common sense that the guy that's keeping track of attendance has noted that you guys are at Pribicevac through the 12th and Zepa, from the 13th through the -- at least the 31st, except for the two guys that went to Trnovo and Kocar, they just stop at the 12th. So isn't this a pretty good indication that you were in Pribicevac until the 12th, Bratunac area, and that from the 13th onward you're at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know the handwriting of the men who did these things in my battalion, but to tell you the truth, I don't remember keeping this document. But I see it's been done with great precision, but what he had in mind when he drew this dividing line at the 12th, we were in Vlasenica on the 12th in the morning fixing our vehicle, replenishing our equipment and our supplies. And in the early afternoon of the 12th, we already set out for Zepa, and for him, when he fills in something in the morning for the next -- or for the next day, that was probably a kind of watershed for him. One terrain was ending, another was starting. It's true that on the 12th in the morning we were in Vlasenica in the corps command, but on the 12th on the afternoon we left for Zepa, and maybe that's what prompted him to do this. If this line is something that he had in mind as something to orient himself by. And I know which of these four men were with me yesterday, and you can also see there were two others, these were young soldiers and I don't remember their names. But every document you show me corroborates what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think we need to argue about that, I don't know if the Court wants to see the original and how it's marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is possible, yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just wonder whether Mr. McCloskey can give us any assistance as to what information the Prosecution have as to who marked it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know who marked it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wasn't asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, all right, then we take it Mr. McCloskey doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're right, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, that was all I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who do you think marked this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I did not know myself that this kind of detailed document was kept, but I can tell whose handwriting this is. Although, it's not clear to me because you see that there is a very gentle handwriting in these boxes. I don't know who could have entered those marking between the 12th and the 13th, just as I don't know who wrote "primljeno" or "predato," "received" or "sent," but I do recognize the handwriting in this document, but I don't know about these markings between the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So whose handwriting do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The handwriting belongs to Bosko Cacic. He was a teacher of the Serbian language in the Rogatica primary school and he was a staff sergeant at the time. I don't know if you need any other information about him. He is my uncle, my mother's brother, by the way. And I kept him with me in the command because he was a teacher and he kept records very punctiliously, as you can see from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree. We agree again. Okay. We are almost done with this topic. Let's go to an intercept, 65 ter 4087. This is an intercept which is short, so you should be able to see the whole thing up on the screen. It's from the Muslims, the fellows at the Konjuh site, dated 12 July. And I want to take you to the second one, it says "zone 2." It is at frequency 255.850, which we know is the RRU-1. And a participant Major Jevdjevic and a switchboard. And Jevdjevic says: "From now on we are going to be at Badem, extension 385, and you can reach Badem through Zlatar." And then they say: "Okay." Where is Badem?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you explain show me the original or a hard copy because this is very pale and I really can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I have got some handwritten notes on the bottom, but I can give you that if it's okay. Now, this is at 1850 hours. Can you tell us where -- what -- what does Badem mean?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Badem is a word I am familiar with. I don't know who it refers to. Zlatar is the Drina Corps command, that I was at 385, that's the extension I described to you. I don't deny that. That was the extension at Pribicevac and at Krivace, the forward command post there. If the date and time are correct, and if the conversation is correctly recorded, but with what switchboard was I speaking? Was it the one in the Drina Corps, then that person would probably have entered it as Zlatar if it was a switchboard in one of the brigades. But it's correct I was at 385, the time 1850, the 12th of July, I was at Krivace at the time. Probably I was informing someone that I had already arrived at Krivace and that they could communicate with me at 385 by way of Zlatar. I've read many of these intercepts, but this one contains very little information. So it's very difficult for me to find my way around it. I am probably telling someone that I am at 385, that's correct, and that they can reach me through Zlatar. So it was someone who needed to be informed that I was at a completely different location and that is consistent with my testimony that I was already at Krivace at that time and I am informing someone about that and that's all I can tell from this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, it says in English: "From now on we are going to be at Badem." And from English we cannot quite tell if you're there at that time or you're going to be there. Do you know from your language and from your memory of this, if any, were you at Badem when you said this or were you going to soon be there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the word "Badem" refers to. I don't know what code name it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get to that, but that's not my question. My question is, wherever this place is, do you remember whether you were there when you said it or whether you were about to be there? I mean, I don't know how Serbian deals with this -- this -- sometimes tenses can be confused.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this could be the code name of some station or centre. I won't go into that. But it jogs my memory. It means from that point on, that was your question, from that point in time I was discussing something with someone, I was conversing with someone. I don't know who, the person listening, I don't know who, I am telling him that I am at a new location. He asked me where I am, I tell him at 385 and you can reach me through Zlatar. Why Badem appears here, I don't know. I can't link it up with everything else, but the other information I have just told you, I can remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about letting him read that and then hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a good point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am going to read this to you in English and see if you think this is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of you reading it, have the witness read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have the witness read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just slowly read to us the intercept as you see it down there, starting with J?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From now on, we shall be at Badem, at extension 385, and you can reach Badem through Zlatar."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's clear, and so you know it's the position of the Prosecution - and I dare say it's been proven beyond a reasonable doubt in Krstic and in Blagojevic - and it's not contested here, sir, that Badem is the code name for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very possible. It was the code name of one of the brigades, and it's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's more than possible, sir. And according to this intercept you're at Bratunac on the 12th of July at 1850 hours.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Bratunac and the switchboard at Bratunac did not have extension 385. Extension 385 existed only at Pribicevac and Krivace. Later on, at Godjenje. It never worked in Bratunac. That's why I said that this information does not tell me -- well, there isn't enough data here for me to be able to interpret this. What is significant here is that I am at extension 385, and you know very well where extension 385 was located, and you know very well that it never functioned in Bratunac but exclusively at Pribicevac, Krivace, Godjenje, and finally at Zlovrh [as interpreted]. That's my response to you, and I am absolutely certain of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't think we can -- any point in arguing over that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- unless Mr. Josse wants to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not really my battle. It's not my battle, Your Honour, but it's simply Mr. McCloskey continually makes speeches of that sort. I show a little bit of exasperation. I apologise. If he's got an answer to what the witness has just said, we suggest he should put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He may -- yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I -- just on this document, it's be called an intercept. It is in fact a report. I wonder if the Prosecution can give us a time that the report was sent on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would suggest you concentrate on what Mr. Haynes has just raised, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am open for questions, Your Honour, at all times. But I think I would rather finish my cross-examination. I will try to look into the document as much as is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's received from the BiH. We believe it to be reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we see the notebook where this intercept was noted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the notebook available, if there is a notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I did not -- did not find it in a notebook. Perhaps as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Haynes points out, it's a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking at the top of -- the top of this, just, I don't want to get into it too much, but it's -- it says "Titanic, 90701, Atlanta," a bunch of numbers. These are things that are said orally over the radio, right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the surveillance group at Konjuh recorded these participants and conveyed this to their superior command and they then informed someone about that in this report -- or, rather, they sent the report on the 27th. They were informing someone. Probably you can see that better at the end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is, I don't think there -- can you tell us -- it sounds like this is coded traffic picked up by the Muslims, correct, verbal coded traffic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I am doing my very best to use all my knowledge and experience from that period, but this looks like a very insignificant intercept from which I can conclude nothing. The participants are 1 and 2. There are question marks next to them. Then he says the conversation was not recorded from its beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Simple question, simple question, is this a coded oral communication?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't remind me of anything. It doesn't remind me of anything from my experience. It's not logical to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we get an indication who identified the witness as the collocatur in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Muslims army, as a start. Let me see if I can go back to the document again. I thought it was over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Shall we have the break now and you try to find this out if it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, we are almost through. Just want to go to another topic now, and hopefully pretty briefly, but this Court has heard evidence about the little gathering that General Mladic had of the staff at the Drina Corps on the evening of the 13th appointing Krstic commander. You surely heard about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the 13th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that in my previous testimony that I -- or I heard that information from another source, because I was at the IKM Krivace on that day. I didn't receive the telegram that the command of the Drina Corps sent out to all the other units about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you what you said in Krstic on this point. And it's at page 7104. You were asked "Do you know what position General Krstic held in the command of Drina Corps to the 13th July, 1995?" And you said: "I think that General Tolimir was the Chief of Staff at the corps." And then you were asked: "Do you have any knowledge as to when General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps?" And you said: "I know that this is an important question, because in my preparations for my testimony here, I read the order of the president of the Republika Srpska dated 13 July, appointing General Krstic commander of the Drina Corps because it is only the president who has the authority to appoint people to these strategic groupings and positions." We heard about that, but you go on: "While we were at Zepa, whether it was over the media or in some other way, anyway, we learned of the decree of the president of the republic. And I know that sometime around the 20th of July, or thereabouts, there was a gathering of generals in the facility close to Han Pijesak. There were a number of generals from the Main Staff and the commanders of the other corps, and also present were General Zivanovic and General Krstic. And I know that the event was organised to observe the hand-over of duty by the commander of the Drina Corps. And I know that after General Krstic's return to the forward command post in the village of Godjenje, some people congratulated him on his taking over of duty. I wish to mention that in that period we were at a location which had very little information outside those related to combat operations in Zepa and around it, and General Krstic himself did not talk about his appointment with us other officers." You never mentioned in your testimony or your statement anything about knowing about the little ceremony that happened on the evening of the 13th. So, sir, as you sit here today do you recall knowing about that ceremony on the 13th or do you stand solely by what I just read?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the meantime, I heard that probably then, too, this information secondhand, that General Mladic lined up some people at the Drina Corps command and said that General Krstic would be the commander of the corps. This is what I heard secondhand. I didn't have that information myself, because at that time I was not in the village of Krivace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you have that information when you testified in Krstic, because you didn't tell us about it in trial? In fact, you said what you just said, you didn't have much information. You guys were dealing with combat.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Everything that I said at that time in the Krstic case was my information that I had had up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So despite the fact that General Mladic appointed Krstic commander on the 13th, you were not aware of it on the 14th, or 15th, or the 16th, or the 17th, or the 18th, or 19th?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have had the information only if I had the specific precise information, and I would have been able to form my opinion on the basis of the actual situation that was then. So if I had testified about something the week before, as far as I was concerned, it was illogical to me, for example, that the new Chief of Staff, Colonel Andric, would lead his hundred soldiers throughout the entire Zepa operation and to have the corps commander, General Krstic, there as well, who was commanding the Zepa operation. And that at that time no one was at the Vlasenica command post to lead the entire corps zone and to deal particularly with the problems that the Zvornik Brigade was encountering at that time. So my testimony at that time was based exclusively on the events that were happening out in the field and the information about the actual situation as it was. In the meantime, and while preparing for testimony in this trial, I really did see the document that the personnel officer of the Drina Corps, on the 13th of July, sent to all the units informing them about hand-over of duty. But this document is something that I just saw a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it's the position of the Prosecution that, given the appointment of General Krstic on the evening of 13 July, you as his coms person, that would have been sending out information under his name as commander and closely working with him, would have absolutely known that he was commander on the 13th or 14th of July and that for you to say anything otherwise is false. What do you have to say about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never drafted the information that you are referring to, because the nature of my duties was such that I was executing the implementation of the communication plan that I would receive from the chief of communications. I never drafted information or had access or an insight into information being drafted by Colonel Vicic or anyone else at the IKM and that was being forwarded to others. So I was not aware about the contents at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 118B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let me give you the -- let me give you the original of that. And maybe I might have got the wrong 65 ter number. But one out of five hours isn't a bad record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could focus on the screen on the B/C/S original. This is a copy of that personnel document that was -- we've seen versions of it before. This one in particular was sent out to your communications battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want you to focus on that handwriting up in the right-hand corner. Isn't that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We didn't get the interpretation for your last comment, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But this is to your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The document arrived at the communications battalion on the 13th of July, and probably on the 14th of July it was logged in at the communications battalion in Vlasenica. The handwriting is by the general affairs desk officer in the battalion, this is the staff sergeant Bosko Cacic, whom we mentioned, so it probably arrived at the battalion in Vlasenica on the 13th of July. And then on the 14th he wrote that here, I mean, there's not that important. I was at the Krivace IKM and I was focused on the Stupcanica 95 operation and the document did not end up on my hands. So I came back from this operation later, about 20 days later, more or less, and I do not believe that 20 days later I went through all the documents. I mean, not that I don't believe that I did that. I know that I did not do that, i.e., look over all the documents that in the meantime had arrived at my units which usually normally functions in my absence. And as I said, this document never did reach the Krivace IKM, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just asked you that because we have what we believe are copies of your handwriting, and that very distinctive swirls and things looks like you, but fair enough. We won't argue over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to some last few intercepts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, if you allow me, sir, if you permit me, please. This handwriting on the screen - and this is why I laughed - is the handwriting of that uncle of mine, who probably has the most beautiful Cyrillic handwriting that I ever saw. I, as a child, learned and practiced to write the way he wrote, and you -- I can give you my notebooks and also his handwriting, his diaries and so on. Many people actually compare the two of us, because I wanted to resemble my uncle. I respect him still today, and you probably looked at my handwriting and this specific letter "P," but actually this is his handwriting and his handwriting is much more beautiful than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let's go to 65 ter 1255C and D. And I can give you a printed out copy of that. It's the one that starts at 2050 hours. There is a couple of them on there, but the one I'm -- this is, just so you know, 18 July as a reference. We won't spend much time with this, but it's -- it's between Krstic, they assume it's Krstic, and an X. And we've heard that your nickname is Jevdjo and --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jevdjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't see that little cross in the D, Jevdjo. And what I want to ask you about is it looks like Krstic is asking if you're around somewhere, and X says: "He is coming down there, too." And Krstic says: "Good, I have to see the man, the KZ." We know that's cryptographic protection. He calls the KZ man an MF. And then says: "I guess we will finally be able to talk to each other. The other one is broken." So did you have some broken KZ protection problems around 18 July that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- we are talking now about this second intercept, right, the other one, which is on the lower half of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me read the conversation and then I may be able to understand something because whoever was intercepting this was assuming that one of the participants was Krstic, and he marked the other one as unknown. He marked him as "X." But I still don't see my name anywhere, but just let me read the conversation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think your name is anywhere. It's just talking about crypto-protection and they think it's Krstic at the command and he's got problems, and perhaps you recall that. If not, we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I remember the situation when Mr. Harmon, the Prosecutor, asked me how many times I went from the forward command post at Zepa to Vlasenica, and I told him I went there once. And he asked me when that was. And I said, more or less the time I needed to take a bath and run some errands concerning the unit. He asked me precisely when that was, and I said maybe it was about ten days of rest. But now I see it was on the 18th. And, yes, I remember this conversation -- or, rather, I remember not this conversation but these activities. So I assume that the conversation is authentic. Can you please put your question to me now, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the KZ equipment not working so they had to bring in the KZ man to fix it, and now you will finally be able to talk protected? When I say "you," I mean the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first, I conclude what whoever was intercepting this conversation, well, he was wrong. This is not a conversation between Krstic and someone else, because it certainly wasn't Krstic who was engaged in this discussion. It shows -- it says here that he should look at this KZ, so it's probably not Krstic, whoever was intercepting this switched things around. We had those cryptographic protection devices in reserve. And I don't think that there's a shred of evidence so far that there was a conversation between Krstic and officers subordinate to him in Krivaja 95 and Stupcanica 95 which was intercepted. If this device was out of order, then everyone in the network would get only a hissing sound, and that would be a signal that the device was out of order and we would immediately intervene and replace it. And maybe this happened just once, but -- among the participants, but we did have reserve devices at the forward command post so as to be able to intervene, and that's all I can say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 1295A and 1295B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, while we are waiting for that document, I was just looking at the document that was left on the screen before the break concerning that intercept in which the participants were not identified. But in that conversation where I am informing someone that we were at Badem at extension 385, I think that that report and the date when this -- if we had the precise date when this conversation was intercepted then we would know precisely when the communications centre at Pribicevac ceased to exist because he said "At 1900 hours, the wavelength ceased to exist," and that was exactly when I switched off my equipment at Pribicevac at 1900 hours. I think that this report was drawn up the previous day. I apologise for taking up your time, but if we knew exactly when this conversation was intercepted, it would be completely clear to you that the communications centre at the forward command post ceased to exist at 1900 hours because it says that in that intercept and it's quite logical that I told someone I was going towards Bratunac, down there, and it would be a very good thing. It would be very important as far as what you are saying goes if we had this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 1295A, 1295B. I think we have got it up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a short conversation where the Palma, which we know is Zvornik, is calling Zlatar and asked if Jevdjevic is on the line, and according to this, Jevdjevic says "yes." Palma says: "Hello, Mr. Jevdjevic, Commander Pandurevic was looking for you," and he asks why the chief up there had been looking for him. This is dated 21 July, by the way. And then Jevdjevic says: "Only to ask what it's like there." And then Palma says: "Jevdjevic, the commander is returning the Krajina men, everything is all right, we repelled today's attacks and are working as planned." Jevdjevic says: "All right, tell him I personally said hello." Palma says: "Everything is engaged, is anything else necessary?" Jevdjevic says: "No." Palma says: "All right. The commander says hello and have a nice day." This appears to be to us that Krstic was looking for Pandurevic, Pandurevic gets back him and asks why Krstic, the boss, the chief, was looking for him. And then Palma reports that the commander -- Pandurevic is returning the Krajina men who were in his zone and that you say to say hello to Pandurevic and then it ends. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that conversation, but I allow that it's very possible. Considering the conversation, my knowledge of the then situation, I allow that it's possible, but I don't really remember this conversation. I was talking to someone in the command of the Zvornik Brigade if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 26th July, 65 ter 1353 A in the English and C in the B/C/S. This is a conversation between Major Jevdjevic and Vinko. And C is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can give you a hard copy if that's easier to read. It's the middle one starting at 0807, 0807 hours. This just is a simple conversation. It appears Colonel Pandurevic is -- he asked early on: "Are they going to ask me to go there?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There are two different intercepts on the screen. The translation doesn't correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, page 2 in the B/C/S where I mentioned the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Vinko who I am interpreting to be Vinko Pandurevic, correct me if you think I am wrong, asks a few lines down: "Are they going to ask me to go there?" 26 July, it sounds like Pandurevic is naturally wondering if he's going to be called to go to Zepa. And later on he says he's been thinking of sending Jovovic or Legenda down there. Do you have any memory of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember parts of this conversation if it was intercepted in its entirety that's possible. I remember some parts of it. The conversation resembles the usual sort of conversation I would have then, a logical conversation between General Pandurevic and myself. The situation reflects what I knew at that time, that is that negotiations were underway, that the guns had been silent for two days, that there was probably an agreement that civilians and soldiers alike should be evacuated from Zepa. I remember that that had been agreed on, and the rest of the conversation is probably something that I need not doubt. Although, some things I find unclear, but as a whole this intercept seems familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the end of July were you still in the Zepa operation, like 29, 30 July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember when members of the Zepa Brigade were going across the Drina over to the Serbian side in large numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that you said Zepa Brigade, I received the interpretation that they were members of the Zvornik Brigade who were crossing the Drina river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. That's one thing we don't have here. Yes, I meant the Muslim Brigade, the Muslim Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had this information at the IKM literally during the last two days of my stay there, at the IKM, meaning my stay there. I recall the events after the evacuation of the civilian population when the Zepa Brigade, for certain reasons, did not wish to evacuate - although I know agreements were reached about this - they probably assessed pursuant to an order or something. So -- and then from the Zepa section they began to withdraw towards the mountain range between Zepa and Srebrenica towards terrain called Zepska Koliba, and the trig point of Zlovrh, and then our units embarked upon a purely military action called "Chasing the enemy." And then I assume that this action lasted for about three days, the 27th, 28th, and the 29th, when our units then came to those elevations of the Zepska Koliba and Zlovrh, where the Zepa brigade put up its last-ditch resistance. And during that process I recall very well Colonel Trivic, the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade was wounded. After that we moved the IKM to the Zlovrh sector itself, for a while the situation was unclear since this is a vast wooded area through which the Zepa Brigade and the units from Srebrenica -- towards Srebrenica, Olovo, and Kladanj, communicated frequently. We didn't have clear information about where they were actually going to. One of the -- among the information was one that the group wanted to break through Radavana Kopusa [phoen], Cina [phoen], Han Pogled, and Olovo, and then we received information that the main part of the Zepa Brigade had descended through the Crni Potok sector and that they had crossed the river Drina in an improvised manner and crossed over to the west bank which is where they surrendered to the border outpost in Serbia. This is the information which I generally have now told you, according to what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at an intercept about -- it's dated 29 July. It's 65 ter 4088. And I've got a simple copy I can give to you. It's printed out. 29 July, 1995. And it's at 255 frequency, so I guess we are talking RRU-1. "Participants, Major Jevdjevic-1?" And they are telling us it's not from the beginning, so they interrupt this conversation, and they catch you at the last -- your last thing is: "To aim across the river." And then one seems to repeat: "To aim across the river?" And Jevdjevic says: "Yes, yes." And then 1 says: "Hello, Rajko, did you understand him, to aim across the river?" And Jevdjevic says: "That's it, that's it." 1 says: "At which targets?" And Jevdjevic says: "The ones he can see. And 1 says: "Which he can see?" And Jevdjevic says: "Yes, the ones he can see well." Number 1 says: "So to aim from the side at targets he can see." Jevdjevic says: "Across the river." 1 says" "across the river? Okay." Jevdjevic says: "And he is on the right side, isn't he?" Number 1 says: "Yes." Jevdjevic says: "Fine, thanks, bye." And 1 says: "Just tell me, who am I talking to." And Jevdjevic says: "Major Jevdjevic." And 1 says: "Okay." So from this it sounds like you're telling someone from the right side of the Drina to fire at targets they can see; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is it those -- the Muslim army that we are talking about that were trying to get across the river?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who are you thinking of, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Zepa Brigade guys that you just told us about, that you were chasing them and they were taking off trying to get away across the river?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Chasing" is a military term for an operation when the enemy is pulling out of the encirclement, and this is how all the units refer to this particular action. This is not persecution or hunting, it's just the same military term as other military terms. This intercept is not something that was monitored from the beginning. I don't know who the other participant is. I don't know who Rajko is. I do remember the action. We, on the right-hand side of the Drina, opposite from Zepa, is the municipality of Visegrad, the territory of Republika Srpska. And we always had a battalion stationed there, a battalion of the Visegrad Brigade, on the right bank of the river. I think we talked about this yesterday, the left and the right bank. Probably you wanted to put that question to me then, and I told you that for the most part of the river Drina, the right bank is Serbia and Republika Srpska is on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not completed. The interpreter has just warned me to slow down because of the interpretation. I think that you recall that yesterday I mentioned that on the right-hand side or the right bank of the river is the territory of Republika Srpska with three municipalities, Rudo, Cajnice, and Visegrad. On the right-hand side of the Drina, opposite from Zepa, we had stationed a battalion of the Visegrad Brigade which was permanently holding those positions, and then from the opposite bank they were able to see better targets of the Zepa Brigade on the left bank which was trying to pull out of our range as we were chasing it. They were able to view better and fire at those targets from the right bank, which is Republika Srpska, to the left bank, which is also Republika Srpska. And this conversation probably refers to the fact that I, since we did not have direct communication with that unit via an intermediary, I was conveying Krstic's orders or whoever's orders they were, to look at and be able to see targets better from the other side of the Drina and to aim at the left bank of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're passing on the order of General Krstic to fire at the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO JEVDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because at the time we had information that a unit of the Zepa Brigade was pulling out through that canyon, through Serbia -- to Serbia, and then we were not able to see them well because they were at a lower point, in a depression, as compared to us. But people on the other side of the canyon were able to see them better. Our unit on the other side of the canyon, and then probably General Krstic, probably conveyed to me, via communications that I should transmit this information to the unit on the right bank, that they should fire at targets on the left bank of the river. This is my interpretation of the conversation. It's a legitimate military act and quite understandable in the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just a last question. You were asked about General Gvero briefly and a specific date was mentioned, 23 July. I want to show you what is a summary of an intercept that we received from the Croatian government on that point and get your comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you do that we hear what Mr. Josse has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I am in the Court's hands. I am going to object to this. We had an advanced warning in the list that this particular document was going to be referred to. I wish to make a submission now. It will take a few minutes, I am bound to say. I'll make it now, because I am wary of what Your Honour had said at page 28756, some weeks ago, that really an objection needed to be taken at the point a particular exhibit was being referred to and relied upon. It's a technical objection, but as I say, it will take me a few minutes to develop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. A few minutes, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: These minutes, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, we've got five.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps five. Again, I am in the Court's hands. It's technical. I don't think it really matters if the witness was to hear this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is this. As my learned friend has just said, this particular intercept comes from a Croatian collection, and if I could start by referring the Court to what Mr. McCloskey said about these sort of intercepts on the 4th of December, at page 29253 of the transcript. My learned friend Madam Fauveau was cross-examining -- or it may have been examining in chief, to be price, and Mr. McCloskey says: "I just wanted to make a point. The intercepts Ms. Fauveau is using are, my understanding, is that they are from the Croatian forces. I don't know a whole lot about them. Frankly, if she can just identify them as from the Croatian forces as each one that's clear on the record, I don't think we are going to have an objection from them. But I think it's important to be able to distinguish between these and the ones that we know so much about." So I accept that there Mr. McCloskey was allowing my learned friend to use the document, but he was advising caution. What we say is this: The Prosecution used a great many intercepts in the course of its case. In relation to those intercepts, the operators were all called to give evidence. They were called in part because the Prosecution initially sought to exhibit the documents through those particular intercept operators. I probably needn't go into this in any detail, the Court is very familiar with this, under Rule 92. And then in the 12th -- on the 12th of September, 2006, this Trial Chamber decided that those intercept operators who gave evidence about intercepts that went to the acts and conduct of an accused person all had to be called. Really, it's our submission that it would be an absurd and perverse result in this case if the Prosecution could now use an intercept that goes to an act and conduct, and this one undoubtedly does. The Chamber may not have seen it yet, but I am sure my learned friend will concede this goes to acts and conduct because it relates to something my client is alleged to have done or places he's alleged to have been on the 23rd of July, if the operator is not called. It would be absolutely, as I say, absurd and perverse result. So it's a technical objection, I accept, but it's an important technical objection bearing in mind how intercept evidence has been presented hitherto in this particular case. And Mr. McCloskey said, rightfully, that one needs to be cautious in relation to these Croatian intercepts s. We say particular caution needs to be given. He may not have taken that point. That was his decision. We do take this point in relation to this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I did not object to the use of those intercepts. That is because I felt they had a sufficient foundation for the Court to be able to gain some meaning from them. And I know more about them now than I did then, but this is cross-examination and we didn't deal with the specific date of 23 July and General Gvero; they did. They brought that up with this witness, and I'm sorry I can't remember all the details on why they did that. But they were clearly making a point. Something to do with Gvero is concerned about the western front, that everybody is going to the western front, which we know is the Krajina. This is a point they specifically made through I think probably ab -- was it an intercept that was or was not in evidence. So they have made that point. That point is sitting there. Now, I have an intercept that responds to that particular day. It's a particular intercept that has to do with Gvero on that very particular day, and I would like to have a chance to question this witness about it. We chose not to use this in our case in chief. We haven't been holding this back. It would never have seen the light of day had they not mentioned this particular date, and then we went and, lo and behold, here is an intercept that helps get us to the truth, I believe. Shouldn't we be able to see it? Can't I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Save the truth point, I accept everything my learned friend has said. It simply doesn't answer the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He has not given one argument, in our submission, as to why I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will come back to you tomorrow morning. We will continue at 9.00. How much longer do you think you will be cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the last intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But still, I assume there will be a redirect, so we have to adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00. Do you have an idea the approximate length of your redirect, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't need a lot of time, Mr. President. If I need to specify the time, perhaps it would be about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will be rather longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be rather long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 15 minutes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we will have most of the day again tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.47 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of December, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
